1: This is the technical deep dive for Book 07 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, P K I and Certificates.
It's for the P K I engineers and architects who will run the move off Active Directory Certificate Services.
Part 1 is hardening and the target: how to make the A D CS that stays the best-defended system you own, then a target of four issuers and one lifecycle platform.

Part 2 is issuing, migrating and retiring: Intune certificate profiles, strong mapping and Entra certificate-based authentication, then coexistence, the six-wave migration, monitoring and retiring the old CAs.
The commands live in the chapters and appendices, marked as illustrative and untested against production.
2: A certificate is a signed claim that's already been handed out.
It sits on devices, smart cards, load balancers and trust stores nobody remembers configuring.
It doesn't move when the directory moves.
It keeps working until it expires, and then whatever relied on it stops.

A D CS is the hardest part of Active Directory to leave: it's wired into the forest, the cloud replacements cover only part of the estate, and domain controllers need certificates as long as they exist.
Meanwhile the rules keep moving, from shrinking public TLS lifetimes to strong-mapping enforcement to post-quantum planning.
So this runs as its own program, because it fails at expiry, not at cutover, often months later and far from the cause.
3: So what does A D CS actually hold up?
The typical estate is an offline root signing enterprise issuing CAs, and every enterprise CA also lives as objects across the whole forest, which is exactly what ties it to Active Directory.
Domain members enroll through autoenrollment and renew quietly in the background.
Chapter 02's inventory has four layers: CAs, templates, issued certificates and relying parties, and the relying parties decide the order of work.
Then every template gets one of four verdicts, asked in order.
Retire, if the consumer is going away.
Migrate, if Cloud P K I or Entra CBA replaces it.
Bridge, if it depends on A D itself, like domain controllers.
And retain what's left, each with an owner and a review date.
4: The migration takes months, and some workloads never leave.
All that time the CA keeps minting credentials the whole environment trusts, so one bad setting can undo every other identity control.
5: The program carries one rule forward unchanged: Critical and High misconfigurations are fixed and verified before any certificate workload migrates.
Migrating from a CA that can be tricked into issuing arbitrary credentials just carries the weakness forward.
And under the bring-your-own-CA model the program recommends, the new cloud issuer chains to the existing hierarchy, so it inherits every weakness on day one.
The ESC labels from SpecterOps' 2021 research are the shared vocabulary, and the book uses them only for defensive checks.
They live in four places: templates, the forest's P K I objects, the CA's own settings, and web enrollment endpoints.
Put a Defender for Identity sensor on every CA that stays.
In G C C, some of these assessments are still preview, so run the manual checks too.
6: The template classes work best as a checklist.
ESC1 is the big one: a template that lets the requester name the subject, allows sign-in, and lets broad groups enroll, so someone could get a certificate in another person's name.
Any single fix closes it, like building the subject from the directory or restricting who can enroll.
ESC2 is a template that allows any purpose to broad groups.
ESC3 is a broadly available enrollment agent template, which you should treat as an impersonation capability.
And ESC4 is anyone other than the P K I administrators being able to write to a template.
One trap when you fix that: if you remove Authenticated Users from a template, give each issuing CA read access, or it can no longer read the template.
7: Next, the directory and CA classes.
ESC5 is write access to the forest's P K I objects, including the NTAuth store that decides which CAs can issue logon certificates.
Write access there is control over authentication, and Defender for Identity doesn't assess it, so review those permissions by hand.
ESC6 is a CA-wide flag that lets anyone supply alternate names on any template.
A common belief is that strong mapping makes it harmless; it doesn't change what the CA will sign, so clear the flag regardless.
ESC7 is broad CA management rights, and remember that service accounts like the Intune connector hold them too.
ESC8 is web enrollment accepting N T L M without protection.
Better still, remove web enrollment wherever nothing depends on it.
8: Every detection in this module depends on evidence, and A D CS produces none by default.
Two settings are needed, and neither works without the other: the CA's own audit filter, and the operating system's audit subcategory for Certification Services.
Turn both on, and test restarts first, because full auditing can slow them on a large CA.
Then watch Microsoft's focused baseline of events: requests issued and denied, revocations, permission changes, CA setting changes, and anyone tampering with the audit filter itself.
Microsoft recommends generating each event in a test first, so an assumed event doesn't become a blind spot.
Forward everything to the sim, and size the local log for the longest outage you can imagine, so evidence isn't overwritten.
9: The program scores each class to set priorities.
To be clear about what's whose: the risk and priority columns are the program's own scoring, and the detection column comes from Microsoft.
Four classes are Critical and Immediate: ESC1, ESC2, ESC6 and ESC8.
Four are High, to fix within two weeks.
One change from the original guide: ESC2 drops from yes to possible for domain compromise, following Microsoft's description of its effect.
Every row is a migration blocker until it's verified closed, and verified has a definition: Defender for Identity shows nothing exposed, plus a manual re-check for ESC5.
That's the record the gate reads.
The first wave doesn't exit until every Critical and High finding is fixed, re-tested and approved.
10: The A D CS that remains may run for years, so strip every template its workloads don't need, keep CRLs publishing on schedule, back up before every change, and treat CA servers as Tier 0, with keys held in an HSM.
Cloud P K I removes most of that attack surface but adds its own.
There's no built-in P K I administrator role, so scope admins with custom roles, keep keys in the TPM, and don't build production CAs during a trial.
Entra CBA is a relying party, so its hardening is about trust and binding: require high-affinity bindings, require CRL checking, and scope each CA to a group.
Scoping mistakes can lock users out, so pilot it.
11: Module 2 is the target P K I.
There's no single replacement for A D CS.
The target is four issuers, each serving what only it can: Cloud P K I, a smaller hardened A D CS, the Federal P K I for piv, and public CAs, with one lifecycle platform holding them together.
12: Cloud P K I is Microsoft's hosted P K I, managed in the Intune admin center.
For device certificates, it replaces the on-premises CA, the NDES server and the connector in one go.
It issues client certificates to Intune-enrolled devices through SCEP, publishes its own CRLs, and hosts up to three CAs per tenant.
Just as important is what it can't do.
It can't issue to anything not enrolled in Intune, and Intune doesn't manage Windows Server, so no domain controller or web server gets a Cloud P K I certificate.
It doesn't do PKCS or OCSP, and a CA's purposes can't change after creation, so plan your three CAs before you create anything.
On licensing and government availability, the slide has the details.
Confirm the entitlement on your current plan.
13: Cloud P K I gives you two ways to anchor trust, and both can live in one tenant.
With a Cloud P K I root, you create the whole hierarchy in the cloud, but every relying party has to be given the new root.
With bring your own CA, you create an issuing CA in the cloud and your existing private CA signs it, so the chain relying parties already trust is preserved.
A few details matter, like making sure the signing CA publishes its chain over HTTP, not just el-dap.
But one consequence outweighs the rest.
Under bring your own CA, the private root's CRL stays where it is, and every relying party, Entra ID included, still has to fetch it.
A root that publishes late breaks the cloud issuer too.
14: A cloud root needs no existing P K I but brings a new chain that has to reach everything.
Bring your own CA preserves the chain you have, makes rollback simpler, and adds one ongoing dependency: the private root's CRL must stay reachable over HTTP.
Neither can serve domain controllers or servers.
For an organization with an established hierarchy and an offline root, the program recommends bring your own CA.
For one building P K I for the first time alongside cloud-first identity, a cloud root removes every on-premises dependency.

Three rules come with the choice: harden the hierarchy before it signs, sign with the root rather than an issuing CA, and treat the root CRL as production, with the next ceremony date recorded ahead of time.
15: Chapter 04 records what A D CS is kept for, and when each use ends.
Domain controller certificates stay until the last domain controller retires, because servers can't get Cloud P K I certificates.
LDAPS, radius and VPN server certificates, network equipment and HSM-held code signing stay too.
That leaves internal server certificates, and the program's decision has three parts.
Internal names come from the retained A D CS, but they're requested and renewed through CyberArk Certificate Manager, so every one has an owner, an expiry alert and automated renewal in one place.
Internet-facing names come from a public CA, through the same platform.
And after Active Directory retires, issuance moves to a standalone CA under the same root, so there's no new root to distribute.
16: piv certificates come from the Federal P K I, and the migration doesn't change that.
The target's job for piv is trust, not issuing.
The federal root isn't in the common trust stores by default, so distribute it to managed devices and domain members, keep NTAuth right while the domain exists, and upload the chain to Entra ID.

Intune handles what it puts on devices, and everything else belongs to the lifecycle platform, CyberArk Certificate Manager, from the program's existing machine-identity vendor, so there's no second vendor.
Its CA account is privileged, so it falls under the ESC7 review.
And because no matching fed-ramp package was listed as of October 20, 2026, the program runs the self-hosted edition inside its own boundary.
17: Module 3 is device and user certificates.
Intune puts certificates on devices, and Entra ID decides whether a certificate proves who someone is.
Those are two jobs that fail differently: one fails visibly, the other can quietly let the wrong certificate pass.
18: Everything in Intune starts with the trusted certificate profile.
It puts the root and issuing CA certificates on the device, so the device can build the chain.
If the device doesn't trust the root, every other profile fails.
Then there are three delivery paths.
SCEP with Cloud P K I, where the device makes its own key, contrary to what the old guide said, and no on-premises servers are needed.
SCEP with A D CS, which runs through NDES and the Intune connector, with the key still never leaving the device.
And PKCS, where the connector generates the key on its own server and hands it over.
That means the private key exists, however briefly, somewhere other than the device.
That trade is why the program prefers SCEP wherever it can.
19: When the issuer is A D CS, the infrastructure rules are strict.
It needs an enterprise CA, and the NDES and connector server must sit in the same forest, apart from the CA and the domain controllers.
Here's the subtle one: the SCEP template lets the request supply the subject, the very setting Module 1 calls dangerous.
It's safe only while enrollment is limited to the NDES service account, so audit that permission like any other, and keep the connector server in the CA's administrative tier.
NDES can't be clustered, so run several identical servers, and watch its own certificates, a frequent cause of outages.
As for which profile fits which use, Wi-Fi, VPN and sign-in certificates use SCEP, and the slide maps the rest.
20: Strong certificate mapping isn't a future deadline; it's the present.
KB5014754 moved domain controllers from matching certificates by name to wanting a strong link to the account, in four steps, ending September 9, 2025.
As of October 2026, every current domain controller is in Full Enforcement, with no supported way back.
One form of that strong link is the account's security identifier inside the certificate.
For Intune SCEP profiles, you have to add it yourself; the old guide said Cloud P K I does it automatically, and Microsoft's instructions say otherwise.
Pilot with a new profile, because editing a SCEP profile revokes what it issued.
Then sweep the domain controller logs to find weak certificates, and read each event's text, because older servers number them differently.
21: Here's how a certificate sign-in to Entra ID works.
The user enters a username, chooses to use a certificate or smart card, and the client hands its certificate to a dedicated Microsoft endpoint.
Entra checks the chain and revocation, finds the matching user, and decides whether the certificate counts as one factor or two.
One practical tip: let that endpoint through your proxies without TLS inspection, or the certificate never arrives.
The trust store is also a blast radius.
Adding a CA lets anything it issues authenticate any user it can be bound to, so add only what you need.
And turn on required CRL checking, because otherwise a revoked certificate still works.
Entra caches CRLs, so when revocation must be immediate, revoke the user's sessions too.
22: Username bindings are how a certificate gets tied to a user.
Some certificate fields are high affinity, because they point to exactly one certificate, and others are low.
The old guide classed issuer plus subject as high; Microsoft classes it as low, because a CA can issue several certificates with the same subject.
And with several bindings, CBA is only as secure as the weakest one.
The program requires high affinity in production and allows a low-affinity binding only in a pilot.
But switching the tenant to high before every user's values are correct locks people out.
Separately, a certificate counts as multifactor only if a pin or biometric protects it, so a piv card qualifies and a software certificate doesn't.
And never target CBA at all users.
23: Staged rollout lets some federated users sign in to Entra ID with certificates while everyone else stays on A D FS.
Microsoft is explicit that it's a temporary testing tool, not a permanent mixed state, and its limits are tighter than the old guide implied, from group counts to how long changes take.
The program pilots with small cloud groups of ten to twenty users, checks the sign-in log to see which binding matched, and grows in steps until the domain converts.
Moving off A D FS doesn't change the credential or the P K I, just where checking happens.
So get trust and binding parity first, keep the staged period short, and back up the farm.
And contrary to the old guide, conversion isn't one-way, as long as A D FS can still be brought back.
24: Module 4 is coexistence, migration and retirement.
Coexistence isn't the last phase; it's the condition the whole project runs in.
For most of the migration both PKIs are production, and the plan has to say which one each certificate comes from, and how to go back.
25: The program runs coexistence on five rules.
One issuer at a time for each use case and population.
Trust goes up before issuance moves.
Revocation is reachable wherever validation happens.
Nothing is revoked just to force a move; certificates are replaced at renewal.
And every move has a tested rollback.
Some things stay on A D CS until Active Directory retires, like domain controller and LDAPS certificates; the old guide said LDAPS could move to Cloud P K I, but an LDAPS endpoint is a server.
radius needs special care, because it must trust both chains for the whole overlap.
And trust runs both ways: the A D CS chain into Entra ID, and the cloud chain into each forest, with NTAuth only for CAs that issue logon certificates.
26: Most coexistence outages are really revocation outages.
Relying parties now sit in three places, inside the network, on the internet, and in Entra ID, and each CA's revocation list has to be reachable from all of them.
The usual trap is an A D CS CA that publishes only over el-dap or an internal address.
Entra ID needs one internet-reachable HTTP address per CA, with no OCSP, and size limits apply.
Fixing that has a twist: the new address appears only in certificates issued after the change.
Entra ID uses its own trust store setting, so sign-in works right away, but other relying parties keep failing until their certificates renew.
The program publishes on plain anonymous HTTP, because Entra ID has to download the list without signing in.
27: The migration runs in six waves, and each wave's exit gate is the next one's entry gate.
The durations are planning figures for a single forest, not commitments, and Appendix A turns each wave into a checklist.
Wave 2 builds the foundation, and it doesn't exit until trust profiles reach ninety-nine percent of managed devices and every CRL is reachable everywhere.
Wave 3 pilots fifty to a hundred devices, with autoenrollment left on so rollback works.
Wave 4 scales in rings, Wave 5 converts the domains while keeping A D FS restorable for thirty days, and Wave 6 decommissions.
And remember, removing or editing a SCEP profile revokes its certificates, so treat profile changes as real changes.
28: Appendix B is the starting matrix that seeds wave 1, and the rule is to classify each template by what it actually issued, not by its name.
A few facts decide most rows.
Cloud P K I issues only to Intune devices, and Intune doesn't manage servers, so every server certificate is bridge or retain, never migrate.
For example, the old guide moved Web Server to Cloud P K I, but web servers aren't Intune devices, so it stays, renewed through CyberArk Certificate Manager.
Some templates even carry two verdicts, migrating delivery while the issuer stays.
Before any migrate row moves, it has to pass four checks, which become wave 4's per-ring exit test.
And every bridge row records the event that ends it, so retirement is scheduled, not forgotten.
29: Migration ends on a date; certificates don't.
Public TLS validity falls to forty-seven days from March 15, 2029, and the design rule is that no certificate may depend on a person remembering a date.

So the target has three renewal engines: Intune profiles for managed devices, A D CS autoenrollment for domain controllers, and CyberArk Certificate Manager for server certificates, each with a named owner.
Neither Microsoft issuer offers ACME, so the lifecycle platform provides it, on its own servers outside FIPS mode.
Drift checks run at least weekly and are kept as evidence, because an assessor asks how long a finding stayed open.
And treat a mismatched identifier in a certificate as a security event, because it can mean the certificate went to a different user.
30: Last, retiring A D CS, the sixth wave.
It applies only to CAs that no longer serve a retained use; domain controllers usually keep at least one issuing CA alive for as long as they exist.
The gate is a finished cutover, a clean thirty-day rollback window, and every retained use running on the CAs that remain.
Then confirm nothing depends on the CA, stop new issuance, back it up, publish a final revocation list, and clean up trust everywhere.
Keep the published endpoints serving until the last certificate expires.
The assessor reads the result as nist special publication eight hundred fifty-three evidence.
So, from Monday: harden first, choose the root deliberately, issue strongly mapped certificates, keep CRLs reachable, and retire A D CS last, with evidence.
